title: Azure Load Balancer: configure and troubleshoot
learningObjective: Configure a public or internal Standard load balancer with frontends, backend pools, health probes and rules, and troubleshoot load balancing failures.
foundation: Azure Load Balancer spreads TCP/UDP traffic across healthy VMs. It works at layer 4: it doesn't look at URLs or cookies.
Public load balancer: internet traffic to a public frontend IP. Internal load balancer: traffic inside the VNet (or from peered/on-premises networks) to a private frontend IP.
engineer: Components: frontend IP configuration, backend pool (NICs or IP addresses in one VNet), health probe (TCP, HTTP or HTTPS, interval and threshold), load-balancing rule (frontend port → backend port, protocol, probe, session persistence: None (5-tuple), Client IP, or Client IP and protocol), inbound NAT rules (port-forward to one VM), and outbound rules.

SKU: Standard (Basic was retired on 30 September 2025). Standard is zone-redundant or zonal, secure by default (backend NSG must allow traffic), supports HA ports on internal load balancers and gives multi-dimensional metrics.

Health probes come from 168.63.129.16 (service tag AzureLoadBalancer). The default NSG rule AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound allows them; a custom deny rule with higher priority breaks probing. Instances failing the probe stop receiving new flows.

Troubleshooting: Health Probe Status and Data Path Availability metrics, Load Balancer Insights, check that the app listens on the probe port/path (HTTP probe needs 200), guest firewall, NSGs, backend in the pool, and that clients aren't backend members calling their own internal frontend (not supported for the same VM).
Choose Application Gateway for layer 7 (paths, TLS, WAF), Front Door for global HTTP, Traffic Manager for DNS-based global routing.

example.title: Three web servers across zones
body: A zone-redundant public Standard load balancer fronts three VMs in zones 1–3 with an HTTP probe on /health. During patching, one VM fails the probe and is removed from rotation automatically; users don't notice.
An internal load balancer fronts the SQL tier with HA ports for an availability group listener.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription and a resource group (rg-net)
permissions: Network Contributor on the resource group
limits: Backend pool members must be in one VNet
HA ports only on internal Standard load balancers
portal: Create a resource > Load balancer: SKU Standard, type Public or Internal, tier Regional.
Add a frontend IP, a backend pool (VMs or IPs), a health probe (HTTP 80 /health), and a load-balancing rule.
Monitor: Load balancer > Insights; Metrics > Health Probe Status.
configuration.cli:
az network lb create -g rg-net -n lb-web --sku Standard --public-ip-address pip-lb --frontend-ip-name fe-web --backend-pool-name be-web
az network lb probe create -g rg-net --lb-name lb-web -n hp-http --protocol Http --port 80 --path /health
az network lb rule create -g rg-net --lb-name lb-web -n rule-http --protocol Tcp --frontend-port 80 --backend-port 80 --frontend-ip-name fe-web --backend-pool-name be-web --probe-name hp-http
az network nic ip-config address-pool add -g rg-net --nic-name vm1-nic --ip-config-name ipconfig1 --lb-name lb-web --address-pool be-web
# Internal LB
az network lb create -g rg-net -n lb-sql --sku Standard --vnet-name vnet-app --subnet snet-db --private-ip-address 10.1.2.10 --frontend-ip-name fe-sql --backend-pool-name be-sql
configuration.powershell:
$fe = New-AzLoadBalancerFrontendIpConfig -Name fe-web -PublicIpAddress (Get-AzPublicIpAddress -Name pip-lb -ResourceGroupName rg-net)
$be = New-AzLoadBalancerBackendAddressPoolConfig -Name be-web
$hp = New-AzLoadBalancerProbeConfig -Name hp-http -Protocol Http -Port 80 -RequestPath /health -IntervalInSeconds 5 -ProbeCount 1
$rule = New-AzLoadBalancerRuleConfig -Name rule-http -FrontendIpConfiguration $fe -BackendAddressPool $be -Probe $hp -Protocol Tcp -FrontendPort 80 -BackendPort 80
New-AzLoadBalancer -ResourceGroupName rg-net -Name lb-web -Location eastus -Sku Standard -FrontendIpConfiguration $fe -BackendAddressPool $be -Probe $hp -LoadBalancingRule $rule

lab.objective: Configure a Standard load balancer and fix four common failures.
steps: Run the default and read why clients are blocked.
Apply 'Probe on wrong port', 'NSG blocks the probe' and 'One VM down'.
Choose a load balancing service: answer every case.
expected: Standard LB needs NSG allow rules

validation.text: Saw a failed instance taken out of rotation
Chose the right load balancing service

lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.cause: Probe port/path wrong, app down, or NSG/guest firewall blocks 168.63.129.16.
troubleshooting.fix: Fix the probe, allow AzureLoadBalancer, check the app returns 200.

troubleshooting.symptom: Clients time out on a public Standard LB.
troubleshooting.cause: Backend NSG doesn't allow the client traffic.

troubleshooting.symptom: Traffic always goes to one VM.
troubleshooting.cause: Session persistence Client IP with few clients, or others unhealthy.
troubleshooting.fix: Check probe status and distribution mode.

troubleshooting.symptom: A backend VM can't reach the internal LB frontend.
troubleshooting.cause: Backend calling its own frontend isn't supported.
troubleshooting.fix: Call the service directly or use a separate client.

comparisons.difference: Layer 7 regional with path routing, TLS and WAF.
AWS layer 4 equivalent; Application Load Balancer is layer 7.

misconceptions.myth: Load Balancer can route by URL path.
Standard LB allows traffic without NSGs.
misconceptions.reality: Standard is secure by default; NSGs must allow traffic.

architectureDecisions: Use zone-redundant Standard load balancers for production.
Use HTTP probes on a health endpoint that checks dependencies lightly.
Use NAT gateway or outbound rules for predictable outbound.

walkthrough.subtitle: Spread traffic across several VMs, and fix it when it stops working.
learn: Frontend, backend pool, health probe, rule

steps.label: One server
steps.title: One web server cannot handle the load, or survive a failure
body: You add a second VM. Now something must share the traffic and stop sending it to a VM that is down.

steps.label: Types
steps.title: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4
body: It balances TCP and UDP traffic, without looking at URLs. A public load balancer has a public frontend IP for internet traffic; an internal one has a private frontend IP for traffic inside the VNet. Standard SKU is the one to use (Basic was retired).

steps.label: Parts
steps.title: Four parts to configure
body: Frontend IP configuration; backend pool (the VMs or scale set); health probe (TCP, HTTP or HTTPS check, every few seconds); load-balancing rule (frontend port to backend port, using a probe).

steps.label: Options
steps.title: Persistence and NAT rules
body: Session persistence: None (spread every connection), Client IP, or Client IP and protocol (keep a user on one VM). Inbound NAT rules forward a port to one specific VM, for example 50001 to VM 1 port 22. Outbound rules give the backend VMs internet access.

steps.label: Troubleshoot
steps.title: Case: the load balancer returns nothing
body: Check: is the health probe passing? (The app must answer on the probe port and path.) Does the VM's NSG allow the traffic, and the AzureLoadBalancer service tag for the probe? Standard load balancers are closed by default, so an NSG must allow the client traffic. Is the VM in the backend pool?

callout.text: All probes failing = no traffic is sent anywhere.

steps.label: Compare
steps.title: When to use something else
body: Need URL paths, TLS termination or a web application firewall: Application Gateway (layer 7, regional). Global HTTP with caching: Front Door. DNS-based global routing: Traffic Manager.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Load Balancer
recap: Layer 4; public or internal; Standard SKU
Frontend, backend pool, health probe, rule
Persistence: None / Client IP / Client IP + protocol
Probes and NSGs are the usual problems

handsOn.title: Balance two web VMs and break the health probe
handsOn.cost: About US$0.05 per hour for two B1s VMs, a Standard load balancer and a public IP. Do it in one sitting and delete straight after.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

A virtual network vnet-lab (10.10.0.0/16) in rg-az104-lab with a subnet snet-app (10.10.1.0/24): Virtual networks > + Create > IP addresses tab. For these labs, untick 'Enable private subnet' on snet-app so lab VMs can reach the internet (in production use a NAT gateway instead).

steps.do: Create two VMs, vm-web1 and vm-web2, in vnet-lab / snet-app (Ubuntu 24.04, Standard_B1s, no public IP, NIC NSG Basic, inbound ports None).

Run a command without SSH: open the VM > Operations > Run command > RunShellScript, type the command, Run. On each VM run the command in the box. It starts a tiny web server with Python, which Ubuntu already has, so no internet access is needed.
steps.see: The command completes. Each VM now serves a page with its own name on port 80.
steps.code: sudo mkdir -p /srv/web && echo "Hello from $(hostname)" | sudo tee /srv/web/index.html && sudo systemd-run --unit web python3 -m http.server 80 --directory /srv/web

steps.do: Search 'Load balancers' > + Create. Group rg-az104-lab, name lb-lab, SKU Standard, type Public, tier Regional.
Frontend IP configuration: add fe-lab with a new public IP pip-lb. Backend pools: add pool-web, vnet-lab, add both VMs' NICs.
Inbound rules: add a load balancing rule: frontend fe-lab, port 80, backend port 80, pool-web, new health probe HTTP port 80 path /. Session persistence: None. Review + create > Create.
On each VM's NSG add an inbound rule allowing TCP 80 from Any (priority 300).
steps.see: Standard load balancers are secure by default: without this the page never loads.

steps.do: Browse to the load balancer's public IP and refresh a few times (or use curl from Cloud Shell).
steps.see: 'Hello from vm-web1' and 'Hello from vm-web2' alternate.

steps.do: Run a command without SSH: open the VM > Operations > Run command > RunShellScript, type the command, Run. On vm-web1 run: sudo systemctl stop web
steps.see: After about 15 seconds every request goes to vm-web2: the probe marked vm-web1 unhealthy.

steps.do: Open lb-lab > Monitoring > Insights or Metrics > Health Probe Status.
steps.see: Probe status dropping for one backend.

check: Traffic was shared across both VMs, then moved away from the failed one.
cleanup: Delete the resource group now: this lab is billed hourly.
When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
